extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of U.S. local government, public administration, and comparative politics; policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Describing and comparing institutional forms, powers, officers, and procedures of local governments (towns, townships, counties, villages, cities) across U.S. states; explains functions, election/appointment rules, fiscal rules, and judicial organization. Useful for analyzing or teaching how local government is organized and operates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Town-to-city transformation and coexistence
rubrics_metrics.description: When a Town reaches a certain population it is usually transformed by law into a City; but occasionally, while the City is created as a municipal corporation within the limits of a Town, the Town continues to exist as a distinct organization (example: New Haven).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that municipal reclassification is typically population-driven; notes possible continued separate town government (mayor, aldermen, common council) alongside town-meeting functions; practical effect may be the town government is dwarfed but remains legally distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Town-meeting powers and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The annual town-meeting of the whole voting population is the central fact in town government and may make orders concerning acquisition, use, or sale of town property; direct officers; vote taxes for roads/bridges/other lawful purposes; institute or defend suits; legislate about noxious weeds; regulate animals; establish pounds; provide public wells; enact bye-laws; impose fines and apply them for town interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies broad local legislative and administrative powers exercised directly by town electors in assembly (example timing: first Tuesday in April); illustrates practical matters handled (roads, animals, fines, public wells, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: County commissioners powers (New England example)
rubrics_metrics.description: County commissioners (chief administrative officers) manage county buildings such as court-houses and prisons; have power to lay out new highways from town to town; to grant licences; estimate amount of taxation needed for county charges; and apportion the county tax among the towns and cities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes commissioners are salaried, limited by statute to well-defined administrative functions, and controlled by the legislature; county authority lacks a legislative assembly and is primarily judicial and highway-oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: County as judicial/highway district (limited authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: The county functions chiefly as a judicial district and a highway district; apart from apportioning county taxes it has no general power over towns and lacks a county legislative assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizes New England counties as of small consequence beyond courts and roads; legislative oversight of counties is by state legislatures rather than county assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Residency and voting eligibility for town-meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Every male citizen of the United States who is twenty-one years old, who has resided in the State a year, in the county ninety days, and in the township thirty days, is entitled to vote at town-meeting; a year's residence in the town is required for eligibility to office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives specific residency durations and age for participation and office-holding in the town-meeting system (periods may vary by state).

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and terms of town officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Town officers include a supervisor (ex officio overseer of the poor), a clerk, an assessor, and a collector (chosen annually); three commissioners of highways elected for three years, one retiring each year; two justices of the peace and two constables who hold office for four years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes staggered terms for continuity, the multiple roles of supervisors, and annual election of many officers; compensation schemes discussed elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supervisor roles and county board membership
rubrics_metrics.description: The supervisor is general manager of town business, ex officio overseer of the poor, a member of the county board composed of supervisors of several towns, and (with assessor and clerk) constitutes a Board of Health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes dual town-and-county function of supervisors and their health/poor-relief responsibilities; the county board aggregates supervisors for county-level administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Town officers’ compensation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Town officers are compensated according to a schedule of fixed fees for specific services, or receive certain per diem wages for time actually employed; the tax-collector's emolument is a percentage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates local variation in pay: fee schedules, per diem, or percentage-based commissions for collectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process to adopt township organization
rubrics_metrics.description: When the people of a county have voted to adopt the township system, commissioners divide the county into towns (conforming with congressional/school townships except in special cases), and each town is invested with corporate capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies democratic adoption by county vote and administrative division aligned with congressional survey; grants towns corporate capacity to sue, own property, and contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Township corporate capacities and central institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Every town is invested with corporate capacity to be a party in legal suits, to own and control property, and to make contracts; the annual town-meeting (first Tuesday in April) is the central fact in town government for election of officers and miscellaneous business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Underlines legal personality of townships and the centrality of the town-meeting for exercise of corporate powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Township/school governance: trustees and districts
rubrics_metrics.description: For school purposes the township is a separate corporation ('Trustees of Schools of Township'); three school trustees are usually elected at town-meetings, hold office three years, can divide the township into school districts; sub-districts elect three directors who control local schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies usual numbers, terms, and powers for trustees and directors; typical township division into nine 2-mile-square districts with local schoolhouses; women eligible to every school office.

rubrics_metrics.name: School operation mandates and taxing limits
rubrics_metrics.description: School directors are obliged to maintain a free school for not less than five nor more than nine months per year, can build/furnish schoolhouses, hire teachers and fix salaries, determine studies, and may levy taxes on taxable property but are forbidden to exceed a rate of two per cent for educational or three per cent for building purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives explicit statutory ranges for school term length and precise maximum tax rates for educational and building levies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of township school funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Township school funds arise from (1) proceeds of school lands given by the U.S. government (interest alone may be expended), (2) state levy property tax of one-fifth of one per cent divided among counties in ratio of population and then townships, and (3) local district taxation for additional amounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies three discrete funding streams and notes restrictions (e.g., interest-only from school lands).

rubrics_metrics.name: County board functions under township organization
rubrics_metrics.description: In counties under township organization the county board is composed of the several town supervisors; it manages county property, funds, and business; erects court-house, jail, poorhouse, and other necessary buildings; levies county taxes; audits accounts and claims; and oversees highways and paupers (in counties not under township organization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains variation: where townships exist, county board is an aggregation of supervisors; in other counties the board may be three commissioners elected at-large; county may assist with important roads and costly bridges.

rubrics_metrics.name: County judicial and court structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Every county elects a judge with full probate jurisdiction who appoints administrators and guardians and has jurisdiction in civil suits involving not more than $1,000 and certain minor criminal cases; the State is divided into judicial districts with circuit courts (three judges per district), appellate courts, and a supreme court of last resort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes multi-tiered court system: county judges, circuit courts attending terms in each county with juries, multiple appellate courts, and final supreme court; indicates types of cases allocated to county judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment and tax equalization procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Taxes (State, county, town) are computed on the basis of assessment by town assessor; assessor, clerk, and supervisor form a town equalizing board to hear complaints and adjust assessments; assessors' books go before the county board for corrections, then an abstract goes to the State auditor and a State board of equalization which adjusts valuations between counties; taxes estimated and collected on finally corrected assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets out multi-level correction/equalization: town -> county -> state, ensuring valuations bear proper relation across towns and counties before tax computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Township as election precinct and election administration
rubrics_metrics.description: In all elections (federal, congressional, State, county) the township constitutes an election precinct, and the supervisor, assessor, and collector sit as the election judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates the township's role in electoral administration and identifies specific local officials who serve as election judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Village incorporation minimums and governance
rubrics_metrics.description: A minimum population of three hundred, occupying not more than two square miles, may by popular vote become incorporated as a 'village' under general law; six village trustees are chosen, they make one president (general duties of a mayor), and may appoint a clerk, treasurer, street commissioner, constable, and other officers as deemed necessary; people may elect a police magistrate with jurisdiction equal to a justice of the peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies numeric thresholds for incorporation and outlines the typical trustee-based governance structure and optional appointment/election of local officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: County officers and functions in Southern States
rubrics_metrics.description: In Southern States the unit is the county (parish in Louisiana) with functions expanded beyond courts and tax collection to include superintendence of public schools, care of the poor, management of roads; county officers usually include board/court of county commissioners, an assessor, collector, treasurer, superintendent of education, overseer of roads, and elected county judges, sheriff, and coroner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes variation by state in titles and powers; officers are salaried and usually elected for one or two years; sheriff often also has law enforcement and executive duties tied to judicial machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variation of township/county importance by region
rubrics_metrics.description: Three broad types: New England (powerful towns, limited county), Southern (county as primary unit, limited smaller divisions), and Middle/North-west (importance of county and active township). In the Middle/North-west the county often appears before smaller divisions and the township has more independence than in the South.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains historical and settlement-pattern reasons for regional differences (e.g., New England settlers vs Southern/Western settlers) and shows tendency for township adoption to grow with population, manufacturing, and desire for education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on township taxation and local debt
rubrics_metrics.description: State laws restrict the amount of taxation and indebtedness towns may incur; examples include very particular provisions limiting taxes and debt so that town-meetings may vote only within statutory limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates that financial autonomy is bounded by state statutory restrictions; town-meetings vote amounts but cannot exceed legal limits.
